overview.title: Decoding a grid of the VAE's 2D latent space; introducing diffusion models
overview.main_topic: Visualizing what a trained VAE decoder has learned by sampling a regular 30 × 30 grid of 2D latent points, then opening section 17.2 on diffusion models via the idea of denoising autoencoders.
overview.central_idea: Because the VAE's latent space is continuous and structured, decoding a regular grid of latent points produces a smooth map in which digits morph into each other. The page then pivots to diffusion models, starting from the oldest strength of autoencoders: removing a small amount of noise (denoising) and super-resolution.
overview.importance: This page closes the VAE story with the payoff that justifies the whole construction (a latent space you can walk through) and sets up the core idea behind modern image generators: denoising, which diffusion models will repeat many times in a loop.
learning_objectives: Read Listing 17.6 line by line and explain how a 2D grid of latent vectors becomes one 840 × 840 image of 900 digits.
Explain why a continuous latent space yields gradual morphing between digit classes and meaningful directions such as 'four-ness'.
State what a denoising autoencoder does and why it is the one task autoencoders excel at, according to the authors.
Describe image super-resolution as an application of denoising and why it matters for the diffusion models that follow.
prerequisites: The VAE built and trained in 17.1.3 (encoder, sampler, decoder; p.537-541)
The idea of a latent space and a decoder/generator (p.533)

summary:
The page opens with **Listing 17.6**, which visualizes the 2-dimensional latent space of the VAE trained on MNIST in the previous pages. It builds a 30 × 30 grid of latent points, with each coordinate spaced linearly between -1 and 1 (`np.linspace(-1, 1, n)`; the y-axis is reversed so that larger `z[1]` values appear at the top). For each grid point it builds a `(1, 2)` latent vector, runs it through `vae.decoder.predict()`, reshapes the output to 28 × 28, and pastes it into the matching tile of a big `840 × 840` canvas (`figure`). The canvas is then shown with Matplotlib in grayscale. The result is Figure 17.5, printed on the next page.

The authors interpret the figure: the decoded digits form a **completely continuous distribution** of classes, and one digit **morphs into another** as you move along a path in latent space. Directions in the space carry meaning (a direction for 'four-ness', one for 'one-ness', and so on). This is the structured, continuous latent space the VAE's sampling and regularization loss were designed to produce (p.536).

After one transition sentence that calls diffusion models 'the architecture behind nearly all commercial image generation services today', **section 17.2 Diffusion models** begins. It starts from **denoising**: you feed an autoencoder a slightly noisy input (for example a low-quality JPEG) and get back a cleaned-up version. The authors call this 'the one task that autoencoders excel at.' In the late 2010s this led to **image super-resolution** models, which turn low-resolution, possibly noisy images into high-quality, high-resolution ones (Figure 17.6, next page). Such models now ship in every major smartphone camera app. The next pages turn this single denoising step into the repeated, loop-based denoising that defines diffusion models.

paragraphs.excerpt: The grid of sampled digits (see figure 17.5) shows a completely continuous distribution
paragraphs.what_it_says: Decoding the grid (Figure 17.5) shows a continuous distribution of digit classes. Following a path through latent space, one digit morphs gradually into another. Specific directions in the space have meaning, e.g. directions for 'four-ness' and 'one-ness'.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Neighbouring latent points decode to similar images, so there are no gaps or regions that decode to garbage between classes. Moving along one direction changes one visual factor (which digit, slant, stroke width) smoothly. This is what 'structured' means for a latent space: geometry in the 2D plane corresponds to variation in image space. In Figure 17.5 (p.543) you can see bands of 7s, 9s/4s, 8s, 5s, 3s, 2s, 6s and 0s, with blended in-between shapes at the borders.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the evidence that the VAE did its job. Sampling any point, even one never produced by encoding a training image, gives a plausible digit. That property makes VAEs useful for latent-space editing and animation (summary, p.561), and it is the general principle of image generation from p.533: learn a latent space where every point maps to a valid image.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Continuity comes from the VAE's two-part loss (p.536). The sampling noise forces nearby points to decode to similar images. The KL regularization keeps the encoded distributions close to a standard normal centred at the origin, so the region around [-1, 1]² is densely used. Note (not in the book): the 'four-ness' direction is the authors' informal way of describing a concept vector. In a 2D latent space only two independent directions exist, so these semantic directions are not orthogonal axes but different headings within the plane.

terminology.meaning: The low-dimensional vector space (here 2D) that the encoder maps images into and the decoder maps back from.
A gradual visual transition from one image to another, obtained by decoding points along a path between their latent codes.
A direction in latent space along which a single semantic attribute (e.g. 'four-ness') changes.

connections: p.536: continuity plus low dimensionality makes every direction a meaningful axis of variation.
p.533: a latent space where any point maps to a valid image is the key idea of image generation.
p.557: text-to-image models also have a smooth latent space that you can walk through to morph between prompts.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The next section covers diffusion models in detail, described as the architecture behind nearly all commercial image generation services today.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This sentence ends the VAE part of the chapter and announces the second of the two techniques covered (p.534 lists diffusion models, VAEs and GANs, and says this edition covers VAEs and diffusion models, since GANs have fallen out of fashion).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It tells you why to care: diffusion models are not a niche technique but the basis of most deployed image generators. They are also the basis of the text-to-image models in 17.3 (p.555).

terminology.meaning: A generative model that creates images by repeatedly denoising, starting from pure noise (defined on p.544).

connections: p.534: the list of the three main families of image generation models.
p.561: the chapter summary calls diffusion models the dominant method of image generation today.

paragraphs.excerpt: A long-standing application of autoencoders has been denoising: feeding into a model an
paragraphs.what_it_says: Autoencoders have long been used for denoising: feed the model a slightly noisy input, such as a low-quality JPEG, and it returns a cleaned-up version. The authors call this the one task autoencoders excel at. In the late 2010s it led to image super-resolution models that take low-resolution, possibly noisy images and output high-quality, high-resolution versions (Figure 17.6). These now ship in every major smartphone camera app.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A denoising autoencoder is trained on pairs (corrupted input, clean target). It learns what clean images look like well enough to undo small, typical corruptions such as JPEG block artifacts, sensor noise or blur. Super-resolution is the same idea with a different corruption, loss of resolution: the model fills in plausible high-frequency detail. Note that the 'autoencoder' here is generalized: there may be no explicit low-dimensional bottleneck. What matters is the mapping from a degraded image to a clean image of the same content.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This paragraph sets up the whole section. A diffusion model is 'a denoising autoencoder in a loop' (p.544). If you know a network can remove a little noise, the next step is to ask whether removing a little noise many times can turn pure noise into an image. The 'one task autoencoders excel at' remark also contrasts with the VAE just shown: plain autoencoders are not good generators by themselves, but they are excellent denoisers.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: a denoiser trained with a squared-error loss learns to predict the conditional mean of the clean image given the noisy one. For small noise, that conditional mean is close to the true image. For large noise it becomes a blurry average, which is one reason diffusion models remove noise gradually, in many small steps.

terminology.meaning: Recovering a clean signal from a version corrupted by noise or artifacts.
Producing a higher-resolution, sharper image from a low-resolution input, by predicting plausible missing detail.
Blocky or ringing distortions introduced by lossy JPEG compression, a typical 'noise' a denoiser removes.

connections: p.543: Figure 17.6 shows a low-resolution image with artifacts next to the crisp super-resolved output.
p.544: the warning that super-resolution hallucinates detail, and the leap to denoising pure noise.
p.336: chapter 11's segmentation models also map images to images; the U-Net used on p.546 was originally a segmentation architecture.

concepts.name: Latent space
concepts.definition: A low-dimensional vector space of learned representations in which each point can be decoded into a data sample (here, a 28 × 28 digit).
concepts.intuition: A map whose coordinates are 'idea knobs' rather than pixels. Turning the knobs smoothly changes the decoded image smoothly.
concepts.technical: In this VAE the latent space is ℝ². Listing 17.6 samples it on a regular 30 × 30 grid over [-1, 1]² and decodes each point with the trained decoder.
concepts.significance: Generation is sampling from and decoding the latent space. Its continuity determines whether new samples look realistic.
concepts.example: z = [0.0, 0.0] might decode to a blend between several digit classes; moving along z[1] might go from 0 to 7 through 6, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9 as in Figure 17.5.
concepts.misconception: That each axis of a 2D latent space corresponds to one digit class. Ten classes are packed into a 2D plane, so classes occupy regions, and semantic directions are generally not aligned with z[0] or z[1].

concepts.name: Variational autoencoder (VAE)
concepts.definition: An autoencoder whose encoder outputs the parameters of a distribution (z_mean, z_log_var) from which a latent point is sampled, trained with a reconstruction loss plus a KL regularization loss.
concepts.intuition: The randomness forces the decoder to work for every point in a neighbourhood, not just exact codes, which fills the space with valid images.
concepts.technical: This page uses only the trained `vae.decoder` sub-model, which maps a (batch, 2) tensor to (batch, 28, 28, 1) pixel probabilities.
concepts.significance: Gives the smooth, structured latent space shown in Figure 17.5, suitable for editing and interpolation.
concepts.misconception: That VAEs are the state of the art for realistic image generation. Their samples tend to be blurry; the book moves on to diffusion models for realism (p.561).

concepts.name: Denoising autoencoder
concepts.definition: A model trained to map a corrupted input (noise, compression artifacts, low resolution) to its clean version.
concepts.intuition: It has seen so many clean images that it knows which details belong and which are corruption.
concepts.technical: Trained on (corrupted x, clean x) pairs with a reconstruction loss. In this section it becomes the building block of diffusion models, and on p.546 it predicts the noise rather than the clean image.
concepts.significance: The authors call denoising 'the one task that autoencoders excel at'; repeating it in a loop is a diffusion model (p.544).
concepts.example: Cleaning up a low-quality JPEG; super-resolving a phone photo.
concepts.misconception: That a denoiser recovers the true lost information. It produces a plausible guess (p.543-544).

concepts.name: Image super-resolution
concepts.definition: Producing a higher-resolution, cleaner image from a low-resolution, possibly noisy one.
concepts.intuition: An artist redrawing a small blurry thumbnail at large size, inventing the fine detail in a way consistent with what such scenes usually look like.
concepts.technical: A learned image-to-image mapping, trained on (downsampled, original) pairs. Missing high-frequency content is predicted from learned image statistics.
concepts.significance: Deployed at scale in smartphone cameras since the late 2010s; it is the direct ancestor of the denoising idea behind diffusion.
concepts.example: Figure 17.6 (p.543): bananas and fruit bowl, from a low-resolution image with artifacts to a crisp version.
concepts.misconception: That it is suitable for forensics. The detail is hallucinated (p.544).

math.title: Latent grid coordinates sampled in Listing 17.6
math.latex: z_{ij} = \left(x_j,\; y_i\right),\quad x_j = -1 + \frac{2j}{n-1},\quad y_i = 1 - \frac{2i}{n-1},\qquad i,j \in \{0,\dots,n-1\},\; n = 30
math.source_text: grid_x = np.linspace(-1, 1, n); grid_y = np.linspace(-1, 1, n)[::-1]; z_sample = np.array([[xi, yi]])

variables.meaning: Number of grid points per axis (30), so 900 latent points in total.
The j-th value of `grid_x`, used as latent coordinate z[0]; it increases left to right.
The i-th value of the reversed `grid_y`, used as z[1]; it decreases top to bottom, so larger z[1] is at the top as on a normal plot.
The 2D latent vector decoded into tile (row i, column j) of the canvas.

math.operations: Linear spacing: np.linspace(-1, 1, n) gives n evenly spaced values with step 2/(n-1). Reversing grid_y flips the vertical order. The tile for (i, j) occupies canvas rows 28i to 28(i+1)-1 and columns 28j to 28(j+1)-1.
math.purpose: To sample the latent plane uniformly over a square window so that the decoded tiles form an ordered map of the latent space.
math.interpretation: Adjacent tiles differ by a latent step of 2/29 ≈ 0.069 along one axis; a smooth latent space means adjacent tiles look almost alike.
math.intuition: Lay a sheet of graph paper on the latent plane and print the decoded digit at every intersection.
math.numerical_example: With n = 30 the step is 2/29 ≈ 0.0690. Tile (i=0, j=0) decodes z = (-1, 1) (top-left); tile (0, 29) decodes (1, 1) (top-right); tile (29, 0) decodes (-1, -1) (bottom-left). The canvas is 30 × 28 = 840 pixels on each side.

code.title: Sampling a grid of points from the 2D latent space and decoding them to images
code.original_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
n = 30
digit_size = 28
figure = np.zeros((digit_size * n, digit_size * n))
grid_x = np.linspace(-1, 1, n)
grid_y = np.linspace(-1, 1, n)[::-1]
for i, yi in enumerate(grid_y):
    for j, xi in enumerate(grid_x):
        z_sample = np.array([[xi, yi]])
        x_decoded = vae.decoder.predict(z_sample)
        digit = x_decoded[0].reshape(digit_size, digit_size)
        figure[
            i * digit_size : (i + 1) * digit_size,
            j * digit_size : (j + 1) * digit_size,
        ] = digit
plt.figure(figsize=(15, 15))
start_range = digit_size // 2
end_range = n * digit_size + start_range
pixel_range = np.arange(start_range, end_range, digit_size)
sample_range_x = np.round(grid_x, 1)
sample_range_y = np.round(grid_y, 1)
plt.xticks(pixel_range, sample_range_x)
plt.yticks(pixel_range, sample_range_y)
plt.xlabel("z[0]")
plt.ylabel("z[1]")
plt.axis("off")
plt.imshow(figure, cmap="Greys_r")
code.what_it_does: Builds a 30 × 30 grid of 2D latent vectors spanning [-1, 1] on both axes, decodes each with the trained VAE decoder, assembles the 900 resulting 28 × 28 digit images into one 840 × 840 array, and displays it in grayscale. The output is Figure 17.5 (p.543).

line_explanations.explanation: Imports Matplotlib's pyplot. `np` (NumPy) and `vae` are assumed to exist from earlier listings (17.2-17.5).
`n = 30` tiles per side (callout: 'We'll display a grid of 30 × 30 digits (900 digits total)'); each MNIST digit is 28 × 28; `figure` is a blank 840 × 840 float canvas.

Callout 'Samples points linearly on a 2D grid'. `grid_x` goes from -1 to 1; `grid_y` is reversed (`[::-1]`) so the first row of the image corresponds to z[1] = +1, matching the usual 'up is positive' orientation.
Callout 'Iterates over grid locations'. Outer loop over rows (i, yi), inner loop over columns (j, xi).
Builds a batch containing one latent vector: shape (1, 2), `[[z0, z1]]`.
Runs the decoder. The output has shape (1, 28, 28, 1), with pixel values in [0, 1] from the decoder's sigmoid output layer.
Takes the single sample (`[0]`) and drops the channel axis by reshaping to (28, 28).

Callout 'For each location, samples a digit and adds it to our figure'. Writes the digit into the tile at rows i·28 to (i+1)·28 and columns j·28 to (j+1)·28 of the canvas, using NumPy slice assignment.
Opens a 15 × 15 inch Matplotlib figure. The name `plt.figure` is unrelated to the NumPy array `figure`.
Computes tick positions at the centre of each tile: 14, 42, 70, ... (`start_range = 14`, step 28, up to 840 + 14 exclusive), giving 30 positions.
Labels the ticks with the latent coordinates rounded to one decimal and names the axes z[0] and z[1].
`plt.axis("off")` hides the axes entirely, including the ticks and labels just configured. That is why Figure 17.5 shows no axes. Delete this line if you want to see the latent coordinates.
Displays the canvas; `Greys_r` (reversed greys) shows high values as white, giving white digits on a black background.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: the trained decoder `vae.decoder` (latent dim 2). Output: a NumPy array `figure` of shape (840, 840) and a rendered plot of 900 decoded digits arranged by latent position.
code.algorithm: 1. Build a regular grid over [-1, 1]². 2. For each grid point, decode to an image. 3. Tile the images into a mosaic preserving grid order. 4. Plot the mosaic.
code.theory_link: This is the 'sample points and map them back to image space' procedure of p.533, run systematically. Because the VAE regularizes the latent distribution toward a standard normal, most of the probability mass lies within a few units of the origin, so the window [-1, 1]² covers a dense, well-trained region.

parameters.name: n
parameters.role: Grid resolution per axis; 30 gives 900 decoded samples.

parameters.name: digit_size
parameters.role: Side length of each decoded image (28 for MNIST).

parameters.name: np.linspace(-1, 1, n)
parameters.role: The latent window being explored. Widening it (e.g. -3 to 3) shows more classes but includes low-density regions where decoding is less reliable.

parameters.name: cmap="Greys_r"
parameters.role: Reversed grayscale colormap: 1.0 is white, 0.0 is black.

pitfalls: Calling `vae.decoder.predict` 900 times with batches of one is slow, because each call has per-call overhead. Batch all 900 latent points into one call (see the illustrative code).
`plt.axis("off")` cancels the tick and label setup above it; the listing's tick code has no visible effect in the printed figure.
The decoder output has a trailing channel axis (28, 28, 1); without the reshape, the slice assignment into a 2D canvas would fail.
Forgetting `[::-1]` on grid_y flips the map vertically compared to a standard plot of the latent plane.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written alternative (not in the book): decode all 900 latent points in ONE call.
import numpy as np
n, digit_size = 30, 28
grid_x = np.linspace(-1, 1, n)
grid_y = np.linspace(-1, 1, n)[::-1]
zx, zy = np.meshgrid(grid_x, grid_y)            # each (30, 30); row i uses grid_y[i]
z = np.stack([zx.ravel(), zy.ravel()], axis=1)  # (900, 2), row-major order
decoded = vae.decoder.predict(z, batch_size=900).reshape(n, n, digit_size, digit_size)
# (n, n, 28, 28) -> (n*28, n*28): interleave grid rows with pixel rows
figure = decoded.transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(n * digit_size, n * digit_size)

deeper.title: Why the map is continuous: the VAE's two forces
deeper.body:
Two parts of the VAE explain Figure 17.5 (p.536):

1. **Sampling noise during training.** The decoder receives a point sampled around `z_mean` (`z_mean + exp(z_log_variance) * epsilon` in the notation of p.535) rather than an exact code, so it must decode a whole neighbourhood to the same digit. Neighbouring points therefore decode to similar images.
2. **KL regularization.** It pulls every image's latent distribution toward N(0, I). This packs all classes around the origin without large empty gaps.

Together, they produce a space where any path decodes to a smooth morph. A plain autoencoder has neither force; decoding a grid of its latent space usually gives many regions of garbage between clusters.

deeper.title: Walking a straight line through latent space
deeper.body: Pick two digits, encode them to `z_a` and `z_b` (use `z_mean`), and decode `z(t) = (1 - t)·z_a + t·z_b` for t = 0, 0.1, ..., 1. Because the space is continuous, you get a smooth animation from one digit to the other. This is the 'latent space–based animation' mentioned in the chapter summary (p.561). Figure 17.5 is all such straight lines at once, along the two grid axes.

deeper.title: Denoiser as a 'cleanup expert'
deeper.body: Think of a restorer who has seen thousands of old photographs. Given a scratched print, they can repaint the scratches convincingly, not because they know what was really under them, but because they know what photos usually look like. That is a denoising autoencoder. The next pages ask: what if you hand that restorer a print that is *entirely* scratches, and let them work in many passes?

misconceptions.claim: The decoded grid shows images from the training set.
misconceptions.correction: Every tile is generated by decoding a latent point chosen on a regular grid; none were obtained by encoding a training image. Most are images that never existed.

misconceptions.claim: The listing's tick labels show you latent coordinates on Figure 17.5.
misconceptions.correction: `plt.axis("off")` hides them; the printed figure has no axes.

misconceptions.claim: Autoencoders are generally poor models, so denoising with them is a toy application.
misconceptions.correction: The authors say the opposite: denoising is the one task autoencoders excel at, and denoising-based super-resolution ships in every major smartphone camera app.

misconceptions.claim: Super-resolution recovers the true missing pixels.
misconceptions.correction: It predicts plausible detail from learned statistics. The next page calls this hallucination.

takeaways: Listing 17.6 decodes a 30 × 30 grid of 2D latent points over [-1, 1]² into a single 840 × 840 mosaic (Figure 17.5).
The mosaic shows a continuous distribution of digit classes: walking through latent space morphs one digit into another, and directions carry meaning such as 'four-ness'.
`plt.axis("off")` hides the tick setup in the listing; decoding one point per predict call is slow, so batch the 900 points in practice.
Section 17.2 starts from denoising, the one task the authors say autoencoders excel at; super-resolution is its most widely shipped application.
Diffusion models, the basis of nearly all commercial image generators, build on this denoising idea.

questions.question: What are the shapes of `z_sample`, `x_decoded`, `digit`, and `figure` in Listing 17.6?
questions.explanation: One latent vector of dimension 2 is decoded per call. The MNIST decoder outputs a single-channel 28 × 28 image per sample; `[0]` and the reshape remove the batch and channel axes; the canvas is 30 tiles × 28 pixels per side.

questions.question: Why does Listing 17.6 reverse `grid_y` with `[::-1]`?
options: So that larger z[1] values appear at the top of the image, as on a standard plot
To make the decoder produce mirrored digits
Because np.linspace returns values in descending order by default
To avoid decoding the same point twice
questions.answer: So that larger z[1] values appear at the top of the image, as on a standard plot
questions.explanation: Image row 0 is at the top. Without reversal, row 0 would correspond to z[1] = -1, flipping the map vertically relative to the usual y-up convention. The decoder is unaffected (not mirrored digits), linspace is ascending by default, and no point is duplicated either way.

questions.question: What property of the VAE's latent space does Figure 17.5 demonstrate, and which part of VAE training produces it?
questions.answer: Continuity and structure: nearby points decode to similar digits, so paths morph smoothly between classes and directions carry meaning. It comes from sampling z around z_mean during training (forcing neighbourhoods to decode consistently) and from the KL regularization that packs the latent distributions around the origin.
questions.explanation: Page 542 states the continuous, morphing distribution; p.536 explains that random sampling around z_mean and the regularization loss force continuity and well-rounded distributions.

questions.question: According to the authors, what is 'the one task that autoencoders excel at', and what kind of model did it give rise to in the late 2010s?
questions.answer: Denoising (turning a slightly noisy input into a cleaned-up version); it gave rise to image super-resolution models.
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the first paragraph of section 17.2.

questions.question: Which line in Listing 17.6 prevents the z[0]/z[1] tick labels from appearing in the final plot?
questions.explanation: `plt.axis("off")` hides all axis lines, ticks, tick labels and axis labels. `plt.figure` only sets the canvas size, `imshow` draws the array, and rounding only formats the tick labels.

questions.question: With n = 30 and the window [-1, 1], what is the latent distance between two horizontally adjacent tiles, and which latent point is decoded in the top-right tile?
questions.explanation: np.linspace(-1, 1, 30) has step (1 - (-1))/(30 - 1) = 2/29. The top row uses the first element of reversed grid_y (+1), and the right-most column uses the last element of grid_x (+1).

questions.question: Can you explain, without looking, how decoding a regular grid differs from decoding encoded training images, and why the former is the better test of a generative latent space?
questions.answer: Encoded training images only test reconstruction at points the encoder actually produces. A regular grid also hits points between and beyond them; if those decode to plausible digits, the space is continuous and usable for generation.
questions.explanation: Generation means sampling new points (p.533); the grid is a systematic way to check that arbitrary points, not just training codes, give valid images (p.542).
